summary: Describes the assumptions, problem statement, and goals for carrying IP over IEEE 802.15.4 networks, which are low-power and small. It lists an initial set of goals, not a final one. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains why carrying IPv6 over small, low-power wireless networks needs special attention. It describes the constraints and lists the work needed to make IP communication practical on those networks.

questions: why is ipv6 hard on ieee 802.15.4
what is a low-power wireless personal area network
subtitle: The assumptions, problems, and goals for carrying IPv6 over low-power IEEE 802.15.4 networks.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.15.4 devices have limited power, memory, and packet capacity, while IPv6 and its supporting protocols require space and resources.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes LoWPAN characteristics and lists prioritized goals, including fragmentation and reassembly, header compression, address autoconfiguration, routing, management, and security.
tldr.outcome: It is an initial problem statement and goal list, not a protocol specification. Some goals are for work beyond the IETF.

today: RFC 4919 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo calls its goals an initial set.

sections.title: What a LoWPAN Is
sections.content:
A Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (LoWPAN) uses devices that follow IEEE 802.15.4. The devices are typically short-range, low-rate, low-cost, and limited in processing power, memory, or energy. Some may sleep for long periods or be placed where they are difficult to reach.

The memo describes both star and mesh arrangements. More capable Full Function Devices can help coordinate and forward packets for more limited Reduced Function Devices. The document assumes applications usually send small amounts of data, though the protocols do not prohibit larger transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: A LoWPAN connects small wireless devices that may have little power and memory. Some devices can help forward messages for less capable devices.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Needs Adaptation
sections.content:
IPv6 is attractive because it provides a large address space, supports autoconfiguration, and connects to existing IP networks. But LoWPAN frames are small, so IPv6 and transport headers leave little room for application data. Mesh routing also needs to keep packet overhead, network chatter, processing, and memory use low.

Other problem areas include simple configuration and management, service discovery, unreliable or sleeping devices, and security. IEEE 802.15.4 specifies link-layer security based on AES, but the memo says it does not define all the bootstrapping, key-management, and higher-layer security details a complete solution needs.
sections.plainLanguage: IP can connect these devices to wider networks, but its headers take up much of a small frame. Routing and security methods also need to fit devices with limited resources.

sections.title: Prioritized Work Goals
sections.content:
The goals share an aim: reduce packet overhead, bandwidth use, processing needs, and power consumption. The highest-priority goal is an adaptation layer below IP for fragmentation and reassembly, because the link can carry much less than the minimum IPv6 packet size.

The next goals include header compression, stateless address autoconfiguration, a mesh routing protocol, network management, implementation guidance, suitable application and higher-layer protocols, and documented security considerations. The list is an initial set and also identifies work that may belong to other standards organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: The first challenge is fitting IPv6 packets into small frames, which requires splitting and reassembling packets. Other goals cover smaller headers, automatic addressing, routing, management, applications, and security.

sections.title: Security Choices
sections.content:
Applications may need confidentiality and integrity protection at the application, transport, network, or link layer. The choice must account for code size, power, complexity, and bandwidth. The memo says a threat model should be developed and names man-in-the-middle and denial-of-service attacks as examples.

Initial key establishment is treated as outside the 6LoWPAN specifications, while later key management and protection of data traffic are in scope for evaluation. Link-layer modes that provide both confidentiality and integrity are preferred over modes that provide confidentiality alone. Network-layer protection may be end to end or limited to the wireless portion, with the latter adding header overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Security needs to protect messages without using more power or packet space than devices can afford. The memo asks future work to weigh those limits against the risks it needs to address.
